title: Hallel (Psalms 113–118)
hookLine: psalms of praise sung on festivals and new moons

cards: Hallelujah. The word turns up far from any synagogue: in hymns, in gospel songs, in Handel's Messiah, in pop songs, in a stadium when the team wins.
It's Hebrew for praise God: hallelu, praise, and Yah, a short name of God. Now take the first half, hallel, and make it a noun.
In Jewish prayer, Hallel is a set of six psalms, the ones brought out for the year's days of celebration.

teach.b: Hallel is Psalms one hundred thirteen to one hundred eighteen, said together as one long song.
It's sung on the three pilgrimage festivals, Passover, Shavuot and Sukkot, on all eight days of Hanukkah, and on Rosh Chodesh, the new moon.
Often the congregation stands, and many communities sing it out loud to lively tunes. The psalms move through a whole story. Praise from the rising of the sun to its setting.
Then Psalm one hundred fourteen: when Israel came out of Egypt, the sea looked and fled, the mountains skipped like rams. Then thanks for being rescued.
And at the end, Psalm one hundred eighteen's great refrain: give thanks to the Lord, for He is good, for His mercy endures forever.

teach.h: THIS IS THE DAY THE LORD HATH MADE.
teach.b: And this line: "This is the day which the LORD hath made; we will rejoice and be glad in it." On some days, like the new moon and the later days of Passover, a shorter version is said, with parts left out.

A well-known reason for the Passover custom, drawn from a Talmudic story about the angels at the sea: the Egyptians drowned in the sea, and one does not sing full praise over the fall of any of God's creatures.
One more telling gap: Hallel is not said on Rosh Hashanah or Yom Kippur.
The Talmud imagines the angels asking why, and the answer is: the King sits in judgment, the books of life and death are open, and should Israel sing?
Hallel knows when to sing loudly, when to sing less, and when to be quiet.

how: Hallel is recited after the morning Amidah on Passover, Shavuot, Sukkot, Hanukkah and Rosh Chodesh, in full or in a shortened form, and it is also sung at the Passover seder.

practice: Find Psalm one hundred seventeen, part of Hallel and only two verses long, and read it out loud like you mean it; or say today's line slowly: this is the day which the Lord hath made; we will rejoice and be glad in it.
Let one reason to be glad about this particular day come up, and if you pray, make it your praise.
